Cornetist Warren Vache is the first major player since Ruby Braff to be inspired by the work of Louis Armstrong. Born in Rahway, NJ, in 1951, he first gained acclaim at a Carnegie Hall concert where he recreated the solos of Bix Beiderbecke. Through numerous recordings on Concord Records, he has kept alive and added to the trumpet traditions established by Louis Armstrong, Ruby Braff, and Clifford Brown. He worked frequently with Benny Goodman and Woody Herman and is a familiar figure in jazz events around the country, often in the company of tenor saxist Scott Hamilton.
Warren was interviewed at Hamilton College on September 23, 1995 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
Good afternoon. We are here today filming for the Hamilton Jazz Archive. We have a marvelous concert in store for us this weekend, and part of that is cornetist Warren Vache. Welcome to Hamilton.
Thank you, nice to be here.
Just flew in from New York on a little by-plane and —
Yeah, your arms are tired. You are a New York area/New Jerseyite.
I was born in New Jersey I now live in Manhattan, yeah. Most of my life I’ve kept a residence in that area, sure.
Was being in that area part of — important for your musical upbringing do you think?

I think it was in the sense that when I was a kid it didn’t make much difference. But as I started to go to college and began working, I had my first gig at 15, and there was quite a lot of activity around Manhattan and New Jersey and Long Island back then. It meant that I worked almost every weekend of my life from the time I was 15 until now. Unfortunately I didn’t do a lot of club hopping when I was a kid, I lived too far away from Manhattan to go in and see that. But later on I was fortunate enough to just catch the end of the club

The club scene, yeah. I mean I worked at Condon’s for four years, alongside Vic Dickinson and two or three doors down the street was Jimmy Ryan’s and Roy Eldridge was there every night. So I was very fortunate to catch that. And that didn’t happen almost anywhere else in the world, you know.
